messages.content:
Terence Tao said:

Thanks to everyone who participated in the Math Distillation Challenge! We hope to run final evaluations and publish the results soon.

In the meantime, I'd like to open this thread for people to share their experiences in this competition, and give any feedback on how to improve the experience for future competitions.

Thank you for running this challenge. What made the challenge attractive for me was the Lean judge with a plain accept/reject, the public reference pipeline that runs locally, the two tracks, and the freedom to submit any program at all. And I enjoyed learning more about universal algebra.

My main observation concerns the "distillation" question itself. I built a single-file solver with no lookup tables and no precomputed proofs.
It scored 200/200 on the held-out stress set in both tracks, with no wrong verdict across more than 3 000 judged problems, and it did so without the LLM.
I measured the LLM stage at the official settings: it never decided a verdict the deterministic part could
not reach on its own, prompt variants made no measurable difference, and on the stress set it was never invoked.
I see this as a genuine result of the competition rather than a failure: it shows where a text-completing model adds no value, and therefore where a next round could look. Two setup choices amplified it. The model sits at the end of the pipeline, called by a Python program to emit Lean text in one shot, and it runs at low reasoning effort with a fixed seed, so it can neither explore nor learn within a problem.

As an alternative setup, the model could lead instead of serve: the LLM would be the agent, and the submission its scaffold, with a Lean REPL and a Python sandbox as tools. I did not try it right now. But basically this is a setup for agentic coding tools use in software development. The judge plays the role of the compiler and test suite, and the scaffold is exactly the distilled artifact the competition was asking for.

I am looking forward to the forthcoming Lean kernel challenge.

messages.content:
Terence Tao dijo:

Thanks to everyone who participated in the Math Distillation Challenge! We hope to run final evaluations and publish the results soon.

In the meantime, I'd like to open this thread for people to share their experiences in this competition, and give any feedback on how to improve the experience for future competitions.

I thoroughly enjoyed this challenge, and will participate in future events. Thanks to all organizers for the work!
The good:

  • Math collaboration has dragged with respect to other disciplines. I am a mathematician, but currently work in CS , where collaboration is not only instant but automated to some degree, and was very excited when I discovered SAIR. To me, mathematics will start to look like these events, hopefully we will have a chalkboard at home still.
  • Not really a competition: Open collaboration was encouraged in forums such as this one. In the view of recent events, I think this is the way to go. If the goal of mathematics is to increase understanding, we need to take part in these human led spaces, no matter what tools we're using.

The bad:

  • Phase 1 was more fun: The prompting challenge cheat sheet was an excellent way to get me invested in the Equational Theories Project, and to hone my LLM usage skills. However, Phase 2 felt more like a vibe coding competition (did anyone write a solver by hand?). Don't get me wrong, vibe coding can be a serious endeavor: one has to build a custom harness, monitoring, unit tests, etc. But at the later stages I was pretty much just throwing Fable at it with the right set of rails and it got to a point of self-improvement. The last 10 days or so I was just grinding random problems from the 22million order 4 implications graph, and telling it to learn from mistakes. I wanted to ask here if someone else had this experience.

Thanks again!
PD: If anyone is working on the finite 677-255 implication let me know. I have some vibe coded partial results. Here's the database https://eq677.icarm.cloud/

messages.content:
Hi everyone! It was an honor to compete alongside so many strong participants, and to finish with 199/200 on all four leaderboards. Structurally, my solver is more of a hand-tuned toy than a polished piece of engineering from top participants; as for method, I wrote a CDCL SAT solver from scratch in pure standard-library Python — very much a triumph of brute force over elegance. For more details, you can see my submission on the leaderboard (EQT02-T00017); I learned a lot from the other published submissions, and thank you all.

What I loved most about this competition was the Zulip: asking questions directly, watching the judging methodology get clarified in public, and learning from other participants' approaches. Also, I'd like to second Axabra's suggestion — any chance we participants could get a shiny, glittering, positively resplendent certificate signed by our co-founders? Thank you! (☆▽☆)

messages.content: By the way, on Zulip, messages about problem clarifications, corrections, and so on are often scattered across different channels and their topics. I would strongly suggest that the @YZ should create a dedicated area where all such scattered updates made elsewhere are reposted in full, which would also make them much easier for us to find. Thanks!
